title: Are Wardrobe Apps Worth It? Who They Help and Who They Don't
h1: Are wardrobe apps worth it? An honest look at time, money and privacy
excerpt: Are wardrobe apps worth it? Who they help, who they don't, and what they cost in time, money and privacy, plus a simple way to test one for a month.
tldr: Wardrobe apps are worth it if you own more clothes than you can see at once, buy duplicates or plan outfits ahead, and will keep the app updated. They rarely help a small, well-edited wardrobe. The main cost is setup time, so test one with your 20 to 30 most-worn pieces for a month before adding everything.
body:
Wardrobe apps are worth it if you own more clothes than you can see at a glance, keep buying things you already have, or like to plan outfits ahead, and if you'll keep the app updated. They're rarely worth it for a small, well-edited wardrobe, or for anyone who won't photograph new clothes as they arrive. For most people the real cost is time, not money.

There's no reliable independent research on how much time or money these apps save, so this page doesn't invent averages. It sets out the costs and the likely benefits so you can run your own numbers.

Are wardrobe apps worth it? It depends on your situation

Your situationWorth it?Why
Clothes spread across a wardrobe, drawers and a spare roomLikelySeeing everything in one place is the main thing an app does
You've bought a third black T-shirt without meaning toLikelyA quick check before buying stops duplicates
You plan outfits for the week or travel oftenLikelyPlanning from photos is faster than pulling everything out
A small capsule wardrobe on one railProbably notYou can already see it all
You wear a near-uniform and like itProbably notThere's little to decide
You won't photograph new purchasesNoThe catalogue goes out of date within weeks

The last row matters most. A catalogue you can't trust gets checked less and less, and then not at all.

The time cost

Setup is the big one. Photographing and tagging a starting set of 20 to 30 pieces fits into an evening if you batch the photos. A whole wardrobe takes longer: in WRAP's 2022 survey of more than 6,000 UK adults, the average person owned 118 items of clothing. At the five items a day that GetWardrobe's setup guide suggests, that's around three and a half weeks of short sessions.

Upkeep is small but never stops: a minute or two for each new piece, removing what you give away, and a tag check when the seasons change.

Whether that pays back depends on what you'd otherwise spend the time on. As an illustration only: if planning outfits on Sunday saved you five minutes on each weekday morning, that's about 20 hours over a working year, against perhaps four or five hours of setup. If you already decide quickly, the time argument doesn't apply to you, and the case rests on money or on enjoying the planning.

Wardrobe size and habits matter more than features

Feature lists are where most comparisons start, but two plainer questions predict whether an app sticks.

How much do you own, and where is it? A wardrobe that fits on one rail is its own catalogue. Clothes spread across rooms, storage boxes and seasonal swaps are where a searchable list starts to help.

Will you change a habit? The app only helps at the moments you open it: on Sunday when you plan, in a shop before you buy, the night before a trip. If you'd rather decide in front of the mirror each morning, and that works, an app adds a step without removing one.

The easiest way to make one stick is to tie it to something you already do, such as checking the app on the same evening each week, or photographing a new purchase before cutting off the tags.

Money: what you pay and what you might save

Wardrobe apps use a few pricing models: completely free, free with a paid upgrade (often with limits on items or features), a monthly or yearly subscription, or a one-time purchase. Prices and limits change, so check the official store listing on the day you decide rather than trusting a review from last year.

The saving comes from what you don't buy. WRAP's survey found that about a quarter of UK adults' clothes (26%, or 31 items on average) hadn't been worn for at least a year. An app can't make you wear those, but it can put them in front of you when you're about to buy something similar. That only works if you look before you buy.

Cost per wear

Cost per wear is the price of an item divided by the number of times you've worn it. A jacket that cost 150 and has been worn 75 times works out at 2 per wear; a party top that cost 60 and was worn twice is 30 per wear. The currency doesn't matter; the ratio does.

Some apps calculate it for you if you log what you wear. GetWardrobe's help pages, for example, describe recording an item's price and purchase date to support cost-per-wear tracking. A spreadsheet with three columns (item, price, times worn) does the same job if your app doesn't, and it's a fair test of whether you'd keep logging at all.

Privacy: what you hand over

A wardrobe app holds more than pictures of clothes. Mirror photos show your face and body, backgrounds show your home, and purchase details show what you spend. Before you add anything, check:

  • whether photos are stored on your phone or on the company's servers
  • whether photos are sent to an outside AI service for tagging or suggestions
  • whether the app shows ads or links to shops, and what data that uses
  • how to delete your account and photos completely

The App Store and Google Play both show a privacy or data safety summary on each listing, and the app's privacy policy has the detail. Our guide to the downsides and privacy risks of wardrobe apps goes further.

As one example of how this can be set out: FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet. It keeps your wardrobe on your device, sends a compressed photo to Google's Gemini API when it tags a piece, and sends item details to Groq when it suggests an outfit, which is why those features need an internet connection. There's no shop and no ads. The full detail is on our AI transparency page.

Who wardrobe apps don't help

Plenty of people are better off without one:

  • Anyone with a small wardrobe they can see in one glance.
  • People who dress the same way most days and are happy with it.
  • Anyone who enjoys choosing in front of the mirror and doesn't feel rushed.
  • People who won't keep up with new purchases, because a stale catalogue is worse than none.
  • Anyone uncomfortable with clothing photos leaving their phone, if the app they're considering stores them online.

How to test a wardrobe app for a month

A month is long enough to know, and you don't need to photograph everything to find out.

  1. Week 1: add a starting set of the 20 to 30 pieces you wear most. Our step-by-step guide to digitising your wardrobe covers photos and tags.
  2. Week 2: use it to plan your outfits for the week on Sunday.
  3. Week 3: open it before every clothing purchase, in the shop or online, and note whether it changes anything.
  4. Week 4: ask two questions. Did you open it without forcing yourself? Did it stop at least one purchase or save you a stressful morning?

Two yeses: add the rest of your wardrobe. Two noes: delete it and don't feel bad, because you've learned you don't need one. If you're still choosing which app to try, the best digital wardrobe apps list compares the main options from their official listings.

faq.q: Do wardrobe apps actually save money?
faq.a: They can, but only if you check the app before you buy. The saving comes from purchases you don't make, such as a duplicate of something already in your wardrobe. There's no reliable independent data on typical savings. A UK survey by WRAP found about a quarter of people's clothes hadn't been worn in a year, which suggests many people own more than they remember.

faq.q: Is there an app that tracks cost per wear?
faq.a: Yes, some wardrobe apps calculate cost per wear if you record each item's price and log what you wear; GetWardrobe's help pages describe this, for example. Features change, so check the official listing. A simple spreadsheet with item, price and times worn does the same job, and trying it for a month shows whether you'd keep logging in an app.

faq.q: Should I sign up for clothing price history trackers to save on a work wardrobe?
faq.a: They do a different job. A price history tracker helps once you've decided to buy something, by showing whether today's price is actually low. A wardrobe app helps you decide whether to buy at all, by showing what you already own. For a work wardrobe, check what you have first, list the real gaps, then use a tracker for those specific pieces.

faq.q: How long does it take to set up a wardrobe app?
faq.a: A starting set of 20 to 30 pieces fits into an evening if you photograph them in one batch. A full wardrobe takes longer: WRAP's survey put the average UK adult at 118 items, which is about three and a half weeks at five items a day. After setup, each new purchase takes a minute or two to add.

faq.q: Are wardrobe apps safe to use?
faq.a: It depends on the app. Check where photos are stored (on your phone or on company servers), whether they're sent to an outside AI service, whether the app shows ads, and how to delete your account. The App Store and Google Play show a privacy or data safety summary on each listing. Avoid mirror photos with personal details in the background.

faq.q: Are free wardrobe apps good enough?
faq.a: For finding out whether a wardrobe app suits you, usually yes. Free versions vary: some cover photographing clothes and building outfits in full, while others limit the number of items or keep some features for paying users. Check the official listing for the current limits. Test a free option for a month first; if it sticks and you hit a limit, a paid plan is an easier decision.
